subject: Communication
title: Inoculation Theory: Vaccines for the Mind
description: A micro-lesson that makes Inoculation Theory: Vaccines for the Mind usable.

hook.text: You can vaccinate people against misinformation the same way you vaccinate against disease: small, weakened doses.

buildup.text: Inoculation theory (McGuire, 1961) exposes people to weakened versions of persuasive arguments so they build resistance.

discovery.text: The game 'Bad News' lets players create fake news. After playing, they're significantly better at spotting real misinformation.

twist.text: Prebunking (inoculating before exposure) works better than debunking (correcting after belief is formed).

climax.text: Google, WHO, and governments now use inoculation campaigns. Short videos teaching manipulation techniques reduce susceptibility.

punchline.text: The best defense against misinformation is a small dose of it, plus the antidote.

quiz.question: Why is prebunking more effective than debunking?
options: Building resistance before exposure prevents belief formation

details.summary: Inoculation theory proposes that exposing people to weakened forms of misinformation, along with refutations, builds resistance to future persuasion attempts. Like a biological vaccine, small doses of the threat develop cognitive antibodies. Research confirms strong protective effects.
details.whyItMatters: Inoculation theory provides a proven method for building resistance to misinformation before you encounter it in the wild.
takeaways: Exposure to weakened misinformation builds future resistance
It works like a vaccine: small doses develop cognitive defenses
Research confirms strong protective effects against persuasion

faq.question: How is prebunking different from debunking?
faq.answer: Debunking corrects misinformation after someone has already been exposed and possibly believes it. Prebunking warns people about specific misinformation techniques before they encounter them.

faq.question: Does inoculation work for all types of misinformation?
faq.answer: It is most effective when the inoculation targets the persuasion technique rather than specific claims. Teaching people to recognize emotional manipulation, false experts, and logical fallacies provides broad protection.
